pages.title: What you will learn
pages.body:
🎯 **By the end of this lesson you will be able to:**
- Brainstorm to bring out the meaning of specialised cells.
- Discuss how specialised cells are formed in dicotyledonous plants and humans.

pages.title: What is a Specialised Cell?
pages.body: A specialised cell is a cell that has developed a particular shape, structure and set of functions suited to carrying out one specific job within a living organism, rather than remaining a general, all purpose cell. Multicellular organisms, such as dicotyledonous plants and humans, are made up of many different types of specialised cells, each contributing its own particular function to keep the whole organism alive and functioning well.

pages.title: Why Specialisation Matters
pages.body: Division of labour, efficiency, and complexity are three important benefits that specialised cells provide to a multicellular organism. Just as a community functions better when different people take on different roles, such as farming, teaching or healthcare, rather than everyone trying to do everything, a multicellular organism functions better when different cells take on different roles, such as transporting nutrients, carrying messages, or producing new offspring, rather than every cell trying to perform every function.

pages.title: How Specialised Cells Are Formed
pages.body:
Specialised cells generally begin as simple, unspecialised cells, which then gradually change in shape, size and internal structure to become suited to a specific function, in a process guided by instructions contained within the cell's genetic material. Dicotyledonous plants and humans both follow this general pattern, though the specific details differ, as summarised in the table below.

| **ORGANISM** | **EXAMPLE SPECIALISED CELLS** | **GENERAL PROCESS OF FORMATION** |
|---|---|---|
| **Dicotyledonous plants** | Epidermal cells, guard cells, cambium cells, xylem cells | Unspecialised cells in growing regions (meristems) divide repeatedly, and daughter cells gradually change in shape and structure to take on a specific role |
| **Humans and other animals** | Nerve cells, blood cells, muscle cells, sperm cells | Unspecialised cells produced early in development gradually change in shape and structure through a process guided by genetic instructions, taking on a specific role |

[[pic:A two panel diagram. The left panel shows a single, simple, unspecialised cell with a plain round shape and central nucleus. The right panel shows the same starting cell branching out (using arrows) into four differently shaped specialised cells, for example a star shaped nerve cell, an oval muscle cell, a round blood cell, and a tube shaped xylem cell, each labelled with its name.]]

Notice how a single general cell type, shown on the left, can give rise to many different specialised cells, each with a distinct shape suited to a distinct function, shown on the right. This transformation from general to specialised is a key concept for understanding how complex, multicellular organisms function.

lessons.subject: sci
lessons.title: How Specialised Cells are Formed in Humans and in Dicotyledonous Plants

pages.title: How Specialised Cells are Formed in Humans and in Dicotyledonous Plants
pages.body:
Every human begins as a single cell called a zygote, which is formed when a sperm cell fertilises an egg cell. The zygote divides again and again by cell division to form a ball of cells that are all alike and are not yet specialised. These are called stem cells. As the embryo grows, groups of cells begin to use different sets of instructions from the nucleus. They change in shape, size and contents and become different kinds of cells. This process is called differentiation. Once a cell has become specialised it usually cannot change into another kind of cell. Some stem cells remain in the adult body. Stem cells in the bone marrow, for example, keep producing new red and white blood cells throughout life.

In a dicotyledonous plant, new cells are formed only in special growing regions called meristems. Meristems at the tips of shoots and roots make the plant longer. The cambium, a ring of dividing cells in the stem and root, makes the plant thicker. The new cells first take in water and become longer. They then differentiate. Cells on the inner side of the cambium become xylem, cells on the outer side become phloem, cells at the surface become epidermal cells, and some epidermal cells of the root grow long projections and become root hair cells.

| **STEP** | **IN HUMANS** | **IN DICOTYLEDONOUS PLANTS** |
|---|---|---|
| **Starting cells** | The zygote and the stem cells formed from it | Cells of the meristems at shoot tips, root tips and the cambium |
| **Cell division** | Makes many cells that are alike | Makes many cells that are alike |
| **Differentiation** | Cells change shape and contents to become nerve, muscle, blood and other cells | Cells lengthen and change to become xylem, phloem, epidermal, guard and root hair cells |
| **Result** | Tissues, organs and organ systems | Tissues such as vascular tissue and organs such as roots, stems and leaves |

pages.title: Going further
pages.body:
> 💡 **Going further**

In both plants and animals, once a cell becomes highly specialised, it usually loses the ability to change into a different type of cell, and in many cases loses the ability to divide as freely as unspecialised cells. This is one reason why certain injuries, such as damage to nerve cells, can be particularly difficult for the body to repair, since these highly specialised cells cannot easily be replaced by ordinary cell division in the way that some less specialised cells can.

pages.title: What you will learn
pages.body:
🎯 **By the end of this lesson you will be able to:**
- Observe specialised dicotyledonous plant cells such as epidermal, guard cells, cambium, xylem from videos and charts, and identify them by their names and shapes.
- Search from books and the internet for information on the functions of the specialised cells of dicotyledonous plants and how they relate to the existence of the plants.

pages.title: What is a Dicotyledonous Plant?
pages.body:
A dicotyledonous plant, often shortened to dicot, is a flowering plant whose seeds contain two seed leaves (cotyledons), and which typically has broad leaves with branching veins, a main central root, and flower parts usually in multiples of four or five. Beans, mango trees, hibiscus and cocoa are examples of dicotyledonous plants commonly found in Ghana. Every part of such a plant, from its outer surface to its innermost tissues, is built from cells that have specialised into particular shapes suited to particular jobs, and this lesson treats each of these specialised cells individually, one at a time, describing its shape, its location, what it does, and how its structure adapts it to that role.

6.3  The Epidermal Cell

pages.title: Shape and Structure
pages.body: The epidermal cell is a thin, flat, tightly fitting cell, usually rectangular or irregular in outline when viewed from above, with very little space between one epidermal cell and its neighbours. Many epidermal cells also secrete a waxy layer, called the cuticle, on their outer surface.

pages.title: Location
pages.body: Epidermal cells form the outermost layer covering the entire surface of the plant, including the leaves, stem, flowers and young roots, essentially forming the plant's skin.

pages.title: Function
pages.body: Epidermal cells protect the plant from mechanical injury, from invading disease causing organisms, and from excessive loss of water through the plant's surface.

pages.title: Adaptation to its Role
pages.body:
The thin, flat shape of epidermal cells allows them to fit together tightly like paving stones, forming a continuous, unbroken protective covering with no gaps for pathogens or water to easily pass through. The waxy cuticle that many epidermal cells produce adds a further waterproof barrier on top of this covering, reducing water loss even further, which is especially important for plants growing in hot, dry environments.

6.4  The Guard Cell

questions.q: Epidermal cells mainly function to
o: Protect the plant's surface from injury and water loss
questions.e: Function Epidermal cells protect the plant from mechanical injury, from invading disease causing organisms, and from excessive loss of water through the plant's surface.

pages.title: Shape and Structure
pages.body: The guard cell is a bean shaped or sausage shaped cell, always found in pairs, with the two cells curving so that a small gap, called a pore or stoma, is left between them.

pages.title: Location
pages.body: Guard cells are found within the epidermis, particularly concentrated on the underside of leaves, where they are interspersed among the ordinary epidermal cells.

pages.title: Function
pages.body: Guard cells control the opening and closing of the stoma between them, regulating the exchange of gases, oxygen, carbon (IV) oxide and water vapour, between the inside of the leaf and the surrounding air.

pages.title: Adaptation to its Role
pages.body:
The paired, curved shape of guard cells allows them to change shape as water moves in and out of them. When water enters and the cells become firm (turgid), their curved shape causes them to bow apart, opening the pore between them. When water leaves and the cells become less firm (flaccid), they straighten and close the pore. This clever, reversible shape change gives the plant precise, adjustable control over gas exchange and water loss, opening the stomata when photosynthesis needs carbon (IV) oxide, and closing them to conserve water when conditions are dry.

6.5  The Cambium Cell

questions.q: Guard cells control the opening and closing of the
questions.e: Function Guard cells control the opening and closing of the stoma between them, regulating the exchange of gases, oxygen, carbon (IV) oxide and water vapour, between the inside of the leaf and the surrounding air.

questions.q: Guard cells open the stoma between them when they become
questions.e: When water enters and the cells become firm (turgid), their curved shape causes them to bow apart, opening the pore between them.

pages.title: Shape and Structure
pages.body: The cambium cell is a small, thin walled, rectangular cell that retains the ability to divide repeatedly throughout the life of the plant, unlike most other plant cells, which stop dividing once they mature.

pages.title: Location
pages.body: Cambium cells form a narrow, continuous layer, called the vascular cambium, found between the xylem and phloem tissues within the stems and roots of dicotyledonous plants.

pages.title: Function
pages.body: Cambium cells divide to produce new xylem cells on one side and new phloem cells on the other side, allowing the stem and root of the plant to increase in width (girth) year after year.

pages.title: Adaptation to its Role
pages.body:
Unlike most specialised cells, which take on a fixed, permanent shape suited to one job, cambium cells remain deliberately simple and thin walled, keeping the ability to divide again and again throughout the plant's life. This retained ability to divide is itself the key adaptation, since it is exactly what allows the cambium to continually generate the new transport tissue a growing, thickening plant needs, which is why dicotyledonous trees, unlike most monocotyledonous plants, are able to grow noticeably wider from year to year.

6.6  The Xylem Cell

pages.title: Shape and Structure
pages.body: The xylem cell (technically a xylem vessel element) is a long, hollow, tube shaped cell with its end walls broken down or removed, so that many xylem cells joined end to end form one long, continuous, unobstructed tube. The side walls of xylem cells are strengthened with a hard, woody substance called lignin, and the cells themselves are dead once mature.

pages.title: Location
pages.body: Xylem cells are found running throughout the roots, stem and leaves of the plant, arranged in continuous strands that connect the root system all the way up to the leaves.

pages.title: Function
pages.body: Xylem cells transport water and dissolved mineral nutrients upward from the roots to every other part of the plant, and their lignin strengthened walls also provide mechanical support that helps hold the plant upright.

pages.title: Adaptation to its Role
pages.body:
The hollow, tube like shape formed by many xylem cells joined end to end, with their end walls removed, creates a long, unobstructed channel perfectly suited to allowing water to flow upward with minimal resistance, sometimes to the very top of a tall tree. Being dead at maturity actually helps this function, since there is no living cell content left to block the hollow tube. The lignin in their walls makes them rigid and strong, allowing them to resist the pressure changes involved in water transport while also supporting the physical weight of the plant.

6.7  Practical Illustration

[[pic:A cross section diagram of a dicotyledonous leaf and stem, with four callout labels pointing to and showing close up shapes of an epidermal cell (flat, tightly packed cells on the surface), a guard cell pair (bean shaped cells surrounding an open pore), a cambium cell (thin rectangular cells in a dividing layer), and a xylem cell (long hollow tube with thickened walls).]]

Notice how the flat, closely packed epidermal cells form a protective barrier, the bean shaped guard cells surround a controllable pore, the thin cambium cells sit in an actively dividing layer, and the long, hollow xylem cells form continuous tubes suited to transporting water upward through the plant.

6.8  Additional Specialised Plant Cells

Beyond the four cells named directly in the curriculum, dicotyledonous plants contain several other specialised cells worth knowing, since they complete the picture of how a plant functions as a whole, coordinated organism.

pages.title: The Root Hair Cell
pages.body: The root hair cell has a long, thin, hair like extension growing out from its main body, greatly increasing the cell's surface area. Root hair cells are found on the surface of young roots, just behind the growing root tip, and their function is to absorb water and dissolved mineral nutrients from the soil. The long, thin extension is the key adaptation here, since it dramatically increases the surface area in contact with the soil, allowing far more water and nutrients to be absorbed than a plain, unextended cell surface could manage.

pages.title: The Palisade Mesophyll Cell
pages.body: The palisade mesophyll cell is a tall, column shaped cell packed with numerous chloroplasts. Palisade mesophyll cells are found in a tightly packed layer just beneath the upper epidermis of a leaf, positioned to receive maximum sunlight. Their function is to carry out most of the plant's photosynthesis. Their tall, upright shape allows many palisade cells to be packed closely together near the leaf surface, while their large number of chloroplasts maximises the amount of light energy the cell can capture, both adaptations working together to make photosynthesis as efficient as possible.

o: Increase surface area for absorbing water and nutrients
questions.e: The long, thin extension is the key adaptation here, since it dramatically increases the surface area in contact with the soil, allowing far more water and nutrients to be absorbed than a plain, unextended cell surface could…

pages.title: The Phloem (Sieve Tube) Cell
pages.body:
The phloem cell, more precisely called a sieve tube element, is a tube shaped, living cell whose end walls are perforated with many small pores, forming a structure called a sieve plate, rather than being completely removed as in xylem. Phloem cells are found running alongside xylem cells throughout the roots, stem and leaves. Their function is to transport sugars produced during photosynthesis from the leaves to other parts of the plant, including the roots and developing fruits, a process called translocation. The perforated sieve plates allow sugar solution to flow from one phloem cell to the next while still retaining enough cell structure to actively assist the movement of sugars, unlike the xylem, which simply relies on a passive, completely open tube.

6.9  Practical Illustration

[[pic:Three labelled diagrams side by side, a root hair cell showing a single long thin extension growing from a root surface cell into the soil, a palisade mesophyll cell showing tall column shaped cells packed with green chloroplasts beneath a leaf's upper surface, and a phloem sieve tube cell showing living tube cells joined by perforated end walls (sieve plates) with an arrow showing sugar solution flowing through.]]

Notice how the root hair cell's long extension, the palisade cell's packed chloroplasts, and the phloem cell's perforated end walls each represent a specific structural adaptation matched precisely to that cell's specific job within the plant.

pages.title: Going further
pages.body:
> 💡 **Going further**

Together, the epidermal, guard, cambium, xylem, root hair, palisade mesophyll and phloem cells illustrate a general biological principle, namely that the shape and internal structure of a specialised cell is very rarely accidental, but is instead closely matched to the specific function that cell must perform, whether that function is protection, gas exchange, growth, transport of water, absorption, photosynthesis, or transport of food.

pages.title: What you will learn
pages.body:
🎯 **By the end of this lesson you will be able to:**
- Observe specialised animal cells such as nerve cells, blood cells, muscle cells and sperm cells from pictures, videos and charts, identify them by their names, and make models to represent their shapes.
- Search from books, journals and the internet for information on these specialised cells and how they relate to the existence of humans.

pages.title: Notes
pages.body:
Nerve cells, blood cells, muscle cells and sperm cells are four specialised animal cells studied at this level, and this lesson treats each one individually, describing its shape, its location, what it does, and how its structure adapts it to that role, before introducing three further specialised cells that complete the picture of how the human body functions.

7.3  The Nerve Cell

pages.title: Shape and Structure
pages.body: The nerve cell, or neurone, has a cell body containing the nucleus, with numerous short, branching fibres called dendrites extending from one side, and one long, thin fibre called an axon extending from the other side, sometimes stretching for a considerable distance.

pages.title: Location
pages.body: Nerve cells are found throughout the brain, the spinal cord, and the network of nerves that extends to every part of the body.

pages.title: Function
pages.body: Nerve cells carry electrical messages rapidly around the body, allowing the brain to communicate with muscles, organs and sense organs, and allowing different parts of the nervous system to communicate with one another.

pages.title: Adaptation to its Role
pages.body:
The long, thin axon of a nerve cell is perfectly suited to carrying an electrical signal over a long distance, sometimes from the spinal cord all the way down to the toes, with minimal delay. The many branching dendrites at the opposite end greatly increase the surface area available for receiving signals from many other nerve cells at once, allowing complex information to be gathered and processed before being passed on along the axon.

7.4  The Red Blood Cell

questions.q: Nerve cells mainly function to
o: Carry electrical messages around the body
questions.e: Function Nerve cells carry electrical messages rapidly around the body, allowing the brain to communicate with muscles, organs and sense organs, and allowing different parts of the nervous system to communicate with one another.

questions.q: The long axon of a nerve cell is adapted to
o: Carry a signal over a long distance with minimal delay
questions.e: Adaptation to its Role The long, thin axon of a nerve cell is perfectly suited to carrying an electrical signal over a long distance, sometimes from the spinal cord all the way down to the toes, with minimal delay.

pages.title: Shape and Structure
pages.body: The red blood cell is a small, round cell with a distinctive biconcave disc shape, meaning it is thinner in the middle than at the edges, rather like a doughnut that has not fully separated in the centre. Once mature, the human red blood cell has no nucleus.

pages.title: Location
pages.body: Red blood cells are found circulating throughout the bloodstream, carried within blood vessels to every part of the body.

questions.q: A mature human red blood cell is unusual because it
questions.e: Once mature, the human red blood cell has no nucleus.

pages.title: Function
pages.body: Red blood cells carry oxygen from the lungs to all the body's tissues, and help carry some carbon (IV) oxide back from the tissues to the lungs to be breathed out.

pages.title: Adaptation to its Role
pages.body:
The biconcave disc shape of the red blood cell increases its surface area relative to its volume, allowing oxygen to diffuse into and out of the cell more quickly than a plain spherical shape would allow. The absence of a nucleus in the mature cell creates additional internal space to be packed with haemoglobin, the protein that actually binds and carries oxygen, meaning the cell can transport more oxygen than it otherwise could.

7.5  The Muscle Cell

questions.q: The biconcave disc shape of a red blood cell mainly helps it to
o: Increase surface area for gas exchange
Move using a whip like tail
questions.e: Adaptation to its Role The biconcave disc shape of the red blood cell increases its surface area relative to its volume, allowing oxygen to diffuse into and out of the cell more quickly than a plain spherical shape would allow.

pages.title: Shape and Structure
pages.body: The muscle cell, or muscle fibre, is a long, thin, elongated cell containing many overlapping protein filaments arranged along its length, which allow the cell to shorten in a coordinated way.

pages.title: Location
pages.body: Muscle cells are found in the skeletal muscles that move the skeleton, in the walls of the heart, and in the walls of internal organs such as the intestines and blood vessels.

pages.title: Function
pages.body: Muscle cells contract and relax to produce movement, whether that movement is walking and lifting objects, the heart beating, or food being pushed along the digestive system.

pages.title: Adaptation to its Role
pages.body:
The long, elongated shape of a muscle cell allows it to shorten considerably along its length when its internal protein filaments slide over one another, producing a noticeable, useful contraction. Many muscle cells are also bundled tightly together into muscle fibres and then into whole muscles, so that the combined pulling force of thousands of individual muscle cells acting together can move an entire limb or organ.

7.6  The Sperm Cell

questions.q: Muscle cells mainly function to
questions.e: Function Muscle cells contract and relax to produce movement, whether that movement is walking and lifting objects, the heart beating, or food being pushed along the digestive system.

pages.title: Shape and Structure
pages.body: The sperm cell has a small, oval shaped head, containing a tightly packed nucleus, attached to a long, whip like tail, with a region packed with energy releasing structures found just behind the head.

pages.title: Location
pages.body: Sperm cells are produced in the male reproductive organs and are released during reproduction, after which they must travel through the female reproductive tract.

pages.title: Function
pages.body: The sperm cell's function is to swim towards an egg cell and fuse with it, a process called fertilisation, which begins the development of a new individual.

pages.title: Adaptation to its Role
pages.body:
The long, whip like tail of the sperm cell beats from side to side, propelling the cell forward so that it can swim the considerable distance needed to reach an egg cell. The energy releasing structures packed just behind the head supply the large amount of energy this swimming motion demands. The small, streamlined head, containing a tightly packed nucleus and little else, reduces resistance as the cell swims and carries only the genetic material needed for fertilisation, without unnecessary bulk.

7.7  Practical Illustration

[[pic:Four labelled diagrams side by side, a nerve cell with a cell body, branching dendrites and a long axon, a red blood cell shown as a biconcave disc in cross section, a muscle cell shown as a long fibre with visible internal striations, and a sperm cell with an oval head and a long whip like tail.]]

Notice how the long, branching fibres of the nerve cell suit it to carrying messages over distance, the simple, round shape of the red blood cell maximises the surface area available for carrying oxygen, the elongated shape of the muscle cell allows it to contract effectively, and the streamlined head and long tail of the sperm cell suit it to swimming.

7.8  Additional Specialised Animal Cells

Beyond the four cells named directly in the curriculum, the human body contains several other specialised cells worth knowing, since they complete the picture of how the body defends itself, reproduces, and keeps its internal surfaces functioning.

questions.q: Sperm cells are adapted for swimming mainly by having
o: A large, round shape with no tail
A long, whip like tail and energy releasing structures behind the head
A nucleus only, with no other structures
questions.e: Shape and Structure The sperm cell has a small, oval shaped head, containing a tightly packed nucleus, attached to a long, whip like tail, with a region packed with energy releasing structures found just behind the head.

pages.title: The White Blood Cell
pages.body: The white blood cell has an irregular, changeable shape and, unlike the red blood cell, retains a nucleus. White blood cells are found circulating in the bloodstream and within the lymphatic system, and are also able to squeeze out of blood vessels into surrounding tissue. Their function is to defend the body against infection, by engulfing and destroying invading bacteria and other disease causing organisms, or by producing antibodies against them. Their irregular, changeable shape is the key adaptation here, allowing them to change form, squeeze through narrow gaps between cells, and surround and engulf invading microorganisms, a process called phagocytosis.

pages.title: The Egg Cell (Ovum)
pages.body: The egg cell is a large, round cell, considerably bigger than most other human cells, containing a substantial store of food reserves and surrounded by a protective outer coat. Egg cells are produced and stored in the female reproductive organs. Their function is to be fertilised by a sperm cell and, once fertilised, to provide the nutrients and genetic material needed for the very earliest stages of development of a new individual. Its large size and stored food reserves are the key adaptations, providing the new, developing individual with an initial supply of nutrients before other means of nourishment become available, while its protective outer coat helps regulate which sperm cell is allowed to fertilise it.

questions.q: White blood cells are mainly adapted to defend the body because they
o: Are fixed in shape and cannot move
Can change shape and engulf invading microorganisms
Carry oxygen more efficiently than red blood cells
Have a long, whip like tail
questions.e: Their irregular, changeable shape is the key adaptation here, allowing them to change form, squeeze through narrow gaps between cells, and surround and engulf invading microorganisms, a process called phagocytosis.

questions.q: The egg cell is adapted for its role mainly by having
o: A large size and stored food reserves
questions.e: Its large size and stored food reserves are the key adaptations, providing the new, developing individual with an initial supply of nutrients before other means of nourishment become available, while its protective outer coat…

pages.title: The Ciliated Epithelial Cell
pages.body:
The ciliated epithelial cell is a column shaped cell with many short, hair like structures called cilia projecting from its exposed surface. Ciliated epithelial cells line the airways of the respiratory system, including the trachea (windpipe), as well as parts of the reproductive system. Their function is to move mucus, trapped dust, or, in the reproductive system, an egg cell, along a surface by the coordinated, wave like beating of their cilia. The numerous cilia are the key adaptation, since their synchronised, sweeping motion can move a fluid layer or an object along the cell surface far more effectively than a smooth, cilia free surface ever could.

7.9  Practical Illustration

[[pic:Three labelled diagrams side by side, a white blood cell shown with an irregular, amoeba like changing outline engulfing a small bacterium, a large round egg cell (ovum) with a visible nucleus and surrounding protective coat, and a column shaped ciliated epithelial cell with short hair like cilia projecting from its upper surface, with small arrows showing mucus being swept along.]]

Notice how the white blood cell's changeable shape suits it to hunting invaders, the egg cell's large size and food reserves suit it to nurturing a new individual, and the ciliated epithelial cell's numerous cilia suit it to moving material along a surface.

pages.body:
> 💡 **Going further**

Together, the nerve, red blood, muscle, sperm, white blood, egg and ciliated epithelial cells illustrate the same general biological principle met in the previous lesson on plant cells, namely that the shape and internal structure of a specialised cell is closely matched to the specific function that cell must perform, whether that function is communication, oxygen transport, movement, reproduction, defence, or moving material along a surface.

o: Complete uniformity of cell shape everywhere
Division of labour and greater efficiency

questions.e: In both plants and animals, once a cell becomes highly specialised, it usually loses the ability to change into a different type of cell, and in many cases loses the ability to divide as freely as unspecialised cells.

questions.e: Function Epidermal cells protect the plant from mechanical injury, from invading disease causing organisms, and from excessive loss of water through the plant's surface.

questions.e: Function Nerve cells carry electrical messages rapidly around the body, allowing the brain to communicate with muscles, organs and sense organs, and allowing different parts of the nervous system to communicate with one another.

questions.q: The long axon of a nerve cell is adapted to
o: Carry a signal over a long distance with minimal delay
questions.e: Adaptation to its Role The long, thin axon of a nerve cell is perfectly suited to carrying an electrical signal over a long distance, sometimes from the spinal cord all the way down to the toes, with minimal delay.

questions.e: Once mature, the human red blood cell has no nucleus.

o: Increase surface area for gas exchange
Move using a whip like tail
questions.e: Adaptation to its Role The biconcave disc shape of the red blood cell increases its surface area relative to its volume, allowing oxygen to diffuse into and out of the cell more quickly than a plain spherical shape would allow.

questions.q: Muscle cells mainly function to
questions.e: Function Muscle cells contract and relax to produce movement, whether that movement is walking and lifting objects, the heart beating, or food being pushed along the digestive system.

questions.q: Sperm cells are adapted for swimming mainly by having
o: A large, round shape with no tail
A long, whip like tail and energy releasing structures behind the head
A nucleus only, with no other structures
questions.e: Shape and Structure The sperm cell has a small, oval shaped head, containing a tightly packed nucleus, attached to a long, whip like tail, with a region packed with energy releasing structures found just behind the head.

questions.q: White blood cells are mainly adapted to defend the body because they
o: Are fixed in shape and cannot move
Can change shape and engulf invading microorganisms
Carry oxygen more efficiently than red blood cells
Have a long, whip like tail
questions.e: Their irregular, changeable shape is the key adaptation here, allowing them to change form, squeeze through narrow gaps between cells, and surround and engulf invading microorganisms, a process called phagocytosis.

questions.q: The egg cell is adapted for its role mainly by having
